items.prompt: Priya is the only person who understands the payments-retry queue. What does that make the retry queue's bus factor?
choices: 6 — the size of the on-call rotation
1 — only one person's absence is enough to stop the team from maintaining it
0 — bus factor only applies to whole teams, not individual systems
Undefined until someone actually leaves the company
items.explanation: Bus factor counts how many people could disappear before a system becomes unmaintainable by the remaining team. Only one person (Priya) has to be unreachable for the retry queue to become effectively unmaintainable, so its bus factor is 1 — regardless of how many other people are technically on the pager rotation.
items.reference:
🧑‍💻 Priya → Retry queue

Why: bus factor = how many people could disappear before the team can no longer maintain the system — here, exactly one.

items.prompt: A team of 8 engineers has a billing-reconciliation script that only one of them, Tam, has ever modified. What's the bus factor of that script?
choices: 8, since the whole team could theoretically read the code
1 — Tam is the only person whose absence would stop the team from confidently changing it
It can't be determined without knowing how complex the script is
4, since half the team could probably figure it out eventually
items.explanation: Bus factor isn't about team size or theoretical ability to read code eventually — it's about how many people currently have working knowledge of the system. Team size (8) is irrelevant here; what matters is that exactly one person (Tam) has that knowledge today.
items.reference:
🧑‍💻 Priya → Retry queue

Why: bus factor = how many people could disappear before the team can no longer maintain the system — here, exactly one.

items.prompt: After the incident, the team pairs Dana with Priya on two real changes to the retry queue, so Dana now also has working context. What happens to the retry queue's bus factor?
choices: It stays at 1 — only the original author counts
It rises to 2 — two people now have working context, so either one's absence alone no longer stops the team
It becomes irrelevant once any documentation exists
It rises to 8, the full team size, since documentation was written
items.explanation: Bus factor moves specifically with how many people have real, working knowledge — not with team size or the existence of some documentation. Dana pairing on real changes is what raises it from 1 to 2, because now either Priya or Dana being unreachable still leaves someone who can act.
items.reference:
🧑‍💻 Priya → Retry queue

Why: bus factor = how many people could disappear before the team can no longer maintain the system — here, exactly one.

items.prompt: The team adds Marcus to the payments on-call pager rotation, but he's never opened the retry-queue code. Does that fix the bus-factor problem?

No — being paged and having working context are two separate things; the pager schedule spreads who responds, not what they know
Yes, as long as the rotation has at least 3 people
No, because bus factor can only ever be fixed by hiring more engineers
items.explanation: A pager rotation determines who gets notified; it says nothing about whether that person has the knowledge to act. Marcus being on the rotation with zero context on this specific system leaves the bus factor at 1 in every way that matters during an actual incident.
items.reference:
📟 On pager rotation
🧠 Has working context on THIS system

Why: these are two separate things — a rotation schedule only guarantees the first one.

items.prompt: What's the difference between 'who gets paged' and 'who could actually resolve this incident quickly'?

'Who gets paged' is decided by a schedule; 'who could resolve it quickly' depends on who actually has working knowledge of the specific system that broke

items.explanation: A schedule assigns responsibility for responding; it doesn't check whether the assigned person has relevant knowledge. Those are genuinely independent — a well-run rotation can still page someone with zero context on the system that's actually broken.
items.reference:
📟 On pager rotation
🧠 Has working context on THIS system

Why: these are two separate things — a rotation schedule only guarantees the first one.

items.reference:
📓 Runbook → Context, on paper, for whoever is on-call

Why: a runbook substitutes for the original author's memory when that author isn't reachable.

items.prompt: In `chargeWithRetry`, what actual condition triggers a duplicate charge?
choices: The payment provider's API silently double-charges on its own end
A confirmation that arrives after the 30-second timeout still gets processed as a success, but the retry had already fired at the 30-second mark and also succeeded
Two customers accidentally use the same credit card number
The retry queue runs the same charge twice due to a typo in the loop
items.explanation: The bug is a genuine race: `Promise.race` treats a confirmation arriving even slightly after 30 seconds as a timeout and fires a retry, but the original confirmation still lands and succeeds too — both charges go through, none of them individually 'wrong.'
items.reference:
t=0s: charge submitted
t=30s: timeout fires → retry submitted
t=34s: original confirmation ALSO arrives → succeeds
Result: 2 successful charges

Why: the retry timer doesn't check whether the original attempt actually failed or was just slow.

items.explanation: The 30-second timeout assumes 'no confirmation yet' means 'the original attempt failed,' but it could just mean 'still in flight.' The missing safeguard is distinguishing a genuinely failed attempt from a slow-but-succeeding one before firing a retry.
items.reference:
t=0s: charge submitted

items.prompt: In the retry-queue's `chargeWithRetry` code, what specifically does `Promise.race` decide between?
choices: Whether to charge the customer once or twice on purpose
Whether the confirmation promise resolves first, or the 30-second sleep resolves first — and treats the sleep winning as proof the original attempt failed
Which payment provider to route the charge through
Whether to log the transaction as successful or failed
items.explanation: `Promise.race` in this code picks whichever resolves first between the real confirmation and a fixed 30-second timer, and treats the timer winning as 'the original attempt failed' — which is the flawed assumption at the root of the bug, since the original attempt might just be running long rather than actually dead.
items.reference:
Promise.race( confirmation, sleep(30s) )
Sleep wins → assumed failure → retry fires
But confirmation may still land later → both succeed

Why: the race treats 'no confirmation yet' as equivalent to 'confirmed failure,' which isn't always true.
